extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature; writers and critics studying heroism and character in history and fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical analysis of what qualities constitute a 'hero' and what makes hero-worship justified or dangerous; useful for writers constructing heroic characters and critics evaluating historical/fictional leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / inarticulate earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: A true hero may be 'inarticulate' — seeming rude, chaotic, or halting in speech — yet possess a deep, genuine meaning and earnestness at heart (e.g., Cromwell: 'a helplessness of utterance, in such bursting fulness of meaning').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate rough or confused utterance with hypocrisy; search lovingly for the real speech 'imprisoned' in broken rude utterances. The printed confusion may conceal a genuine inward sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in Providence / conviction of divine guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders who conceive their actions as 'births of Providence' — attributing events and victories to divine guidance rather than theatrical contrivance — show a foundational orientation to meaning larger than themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the figure frames events as providential rather than merely tactical or self-aggrandizing; this conviction gives moral weight and resoluteness to action (Cromwell's insistence that events were not precontrived but guided by God).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over pedantry / practical orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic stature is shown by acting decisively in reality rather than being constrained by constitutional niceties, pedantries or purely rhetorical/legalistic argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the subject prioritizes concrete, effective action ('to act it rather') instead of getting lost in 'idle pedantries' and 'bottomless cavillings'; practical accomplishment counts more than formalistic procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating inspiration into institutions / capacity to organize
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero not only experiences high convictions but helps translate them into organized, feasible arrangements (e.g., turning 'Christ's Law' into the Law of the land through counsel and institution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ability to take visionary impulse and shape it into governance, laws, or institutions — the capacity to 'assemble together, and say in what manner all this could be organized.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unwillingness or inability to resign when cause threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine leader 'could not get resigned' — once embarked on a cause, retreat is impossible because resignation would invite countervailing forces to destroy both the cause and the man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the subject's commitment level and whether their refusal to abandon a cause stems from responsibility toward a wider movement rather than mere pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective and moral governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic rule involves concrete moral acts: protecting the oppressed abroad, appointing just judges, fostering true ministers, and striving to make the polity morally better ('cherishing true Gospel ministers; doing the best I can to make England a Christian England').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a leader's heroism by tangible policies and appointments that aim at justice and moral improvement, not merely grand rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of symbolism / congruence of rites with reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols and ceremonies accompanying a hero must be genuinely connected to the real basis of their power (Cromwell's 'Sword and Bible' vs Napoleon's theatrical coronation and P ope's-Concordat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inaugurations and symbols that honestly reflect how authority was won and exercised rather than theatrical borrowings that mask inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding in reality / facts versus semblance
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful hero is grounded in 'reality and Fact' rather than in 'semblance and Sham'; orientation to the practical heart of matters and to verifiable fact underpins durable greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether actions and claims are rooted in tangible facts and practical sensing of the situation ('the practical heart of the matter') rather than theatrical or purely rhetorical displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and avoidance of lies
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling lies (e.g., Napoleon's false bulletins) is morally wrong and tactically ruinous: once lies are exposed, future important truths will not be believed ('The old cry of wolf!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess credibility: habitual misinformation destroys long-term authority. Leaders should avoid falsehoods even for short-term advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive discernment of nature / practical intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero may possess a native instinct for 'Nature' and practical discernment (Napoleon's instinct to test the upholstery and notice tinsel) that lets them perceive truth beneath appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value demonstrations of practical intuition and rapid appraisal of what is real versus superficial, especially in moments of contingency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing faith in movement with hatred of anarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic statesman can embrace a large emancipatory force (e.g., Democracy) while hating and resisting anarchy; they aim to 'tame' and make the movement organic so it can endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for leaders who combine enthusiasm for transformative change with structures of authority and order that prevent self-destruction of the movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of tyrannous injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievous injustices and tyrannies (such as murdering innocents) provoke deep, long-term hostility and contribute decisively to a leader's downfall ('Injustice pays itself with frightful compound-interest').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the subject refrains from gratuitous cruelties; single notorious injustices can undermine legitimacy and fuel resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to charlatan-element / danger of theatrical self-deception
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a 'charlatan-element' — theatricality, self-deception, and adoption of false costumes of authority — which, once developed, makes achievements transient and leads to ruin (Napoleon's adoption of dynasties and pageantry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose signs of theatrical self-fashioning or self-deception; durable greatness requires resisting the temptation to substitute semblance for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure by what Nature will sanction / permanence tied to justice and reality
rubrics_metrics.description: What ultimately endures is what accords with Nature and justice; the 'rest was all smoke and waste' compared to what was real and just in a leader's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate long-term significance by asking what aspects of a leader's work will be sanctioned and sustained by moral and natural justice rather than ephemeral spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of speech when action is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: If speech cannot produce practical result, it is better to remain silent ('Say nothing, if one can do nothing!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words as instruments toward effect; verbosity without capacity to act is a negative trait in a leader or heroic figure.
